rv.q: It could have been blandly affectionate, but there's a keen intelligence and disquieting darkness behind the laughs.
It's as much tribute act as drama, the chief pleasure of which is to see these stars of (some of) our childhoods brought uncannily back to life.

Thanks to the casual, lived-in feel of the dynamics conjured by the three actors, the production works best as a semi-dramatised masterclass on differing comic styles – including a nice section on how each walks differently through an onstage gate.

But mostly it’s just a chortling, smug, snoozefest, with moments of seriousness heavily flagged by flickering bulbs and the kind of “thoom” sound effect that usually accompanies a nuclear explosion in films.

Above all else (as I’m sure the three would agree) we’re indulged in the incomparable pleasure, that greatest of therapies, the opportunity to sit in a room and laugh and laugh and laugh in commune with the men who sacrificed much for that rare, joyous and uniquely human(e) experience.
This is a welcome chance to remember what made them so beloved, and at a brisk 80 minutes, it leaves you aching for more – just like the comics themselves.
The Last Laugh is a fantastic, nostalgic, and laugh-out-loud show that had a sell-out run at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival before coming to the London stage.
The show does well to satisfy both camps.

The comedy simply serves as a steer to a joyous jaunt down memory lane whilst hinting gently at the pathos and tragedy which is never far from the surface of those who are born to make others laugh, often at the expense of their own health and sanity.

cn.t: Pitch-perfect impersonations and nostalgic charm delight in this imagined meeting of Cooper, Morecambe and Monkhouse, though critics split on whether the script offers substance beyond sentimental tribute and recycled gags.
